title: Fast Following: Military Emulation and Twenty-First-Century Transformation
gist: CSIS argues that 'fast following' (copying, improving and fielding an innovation someone else has proven) is now a core military competency, traced through the Shahed's path from Iran to Russia to the U.S. LUCAS and back to Iran, Ukraine-Russia copying cycles measured in weeks, and Western Pacific militaries emulating wars they have not fought. The demonstration-to-adoption gap is driven by institutions rather than technology: weeks for Ukraine and Russia, about 18 months for Hezbollah, about 3.5 years for the U.S. The report recommends intermediaries, rapid acquisition, embedding Ukrainian expertise and measuring that gap.

themes.theme: Fast following as a strategic framework

insights.claim: Fast following, deliberately observing an innovation proven by someone else then copying, improving and fielding it at speed, is now a core competency for military institutions, yet few Western militaries have built a systemic capacity for it while their adversaries have.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Defense procurement may shift toward rapid adoption of proven, cheap systems rather than exquisite first-of-kind platforms.
insights.quote: Western military institutions have invested heavily in innovation units, experimentation, and technology development. Far fewer have built a deliberate and systemic capacity to fast follow.
insights.locator: The central argument of this report

insights.claim: Business research shows first movers fail about 47 percent of the time versus an 8 percent failure rate for early followers, per Golder and Tellis's study of 500 brands, and Lieberman and Montgomery later conceded going first was riskier than they claimed.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Supports fast-follower strategies in sectors with low copying barriers, including defense tech and drones.
insights.locator: The evidence that emerged subsequently

insights.claim: War strips away the patent, capital and long-product-life protections that sustain first-mover advantage in business, making fast following the normal condition of military competition.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Defense innovators in drones and EW face rapidly eroding technical moats; scale and iteration speed matter more than IP.
insights.locator: A fast follower’s advantage is contingent

insights.claim: Horowitz's demonstration point, when an innovation's potential becomes known through a first mover's use, is now reached faster and more widely observed as combat imagery posts online within hours and open-source analysts dissect weapons within days.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Faster diffusion compresses the commercial life of any single drone or counter-drone design.

insights.claim: China, Russia, Iran and North Korea operate as an integrated collective fast-following bloc, so lessons learned in one theater must be assumed available to all bloc members in every theater.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Raises threat assumptions for Indo-Pacific planning and supports sustained Western counter-drone and air-defense spending.
insights.quote: For Western planners, this means that lessons learned in one theater must be assumed to be available to all members of the bloc in every theater.

insights.claim: Russia localized Iran's Shahed-136 as the Geran-2, produced it in the tens of thousands and iterated jet-powered variants like the Geran-5 with anti-jamming antennas, mesh modems and air-to-air missiles, with operator-to-engineer loops measured in weeks.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Mass-produced cheap strike drones drive sustained global demand for low-cost interceptors and air defense.
insights.locator: Russia as a Fast Follower

insights.claim: Russia copied Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces within 18 months, standing up its own branch in November 2025, which had about 101,000 personnel by April 2026 with plans for 165,500 by end-2026.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Russia's drone force scale is outpacing Ukraine and most Western militaries, a driver of European drone and counter-drone budgets.
insights.locator: The scale and reach of Russia’s institutional

insights.claim: Russia's Rubicon Center, established August 2024 as a doctrinal laboratory in response to Ukrainian drone units, conducted thousands of strikes on Ukrainian logistics and drone crews.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Shows institutional innovation, not just hardware, determines battlefield drone effectiveness.
insights.locator: Russia once again fast followed

insights.claim: Russia's copying of Ukraine's use of Starlink via gray-market terminals collapsed almost overnight in February 2026 when SpaceX and Ukraine's defense ministry introduced a whitelist, enabling Ukrainian advances in the south.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Commercial satellite operators wield decisive battlefield leverage, highlighting strategic value of controlled-access space networks.
insights.quote: A fast follower that emulates a capability built on someone else’s infrastructure inherits that infrastructure’s strengths and its vulnerabilities.
insights.locator: But the advantage in drone technology

insights.claim: After Russia demonstrated fiber-optic FPV drones at Kursk in August 2024, Ukrainian manufacturers copied and improved them within months, reaching ranges up to 30 kilometers.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Jamming-immune drones diminish the value of RF-based electronic warfare, shifting counter-drone demand toward kinetic and other solutions.
insights.locator: Ukraine as a Fast Follower

insights.claim: In April 2026 a Ukrainian manufacturer unveiled the Khmarynka, a 50-kilometer-range fixed-wing strike drone with a 7-kilogram payload resembling Russia's Molniya, offered via the Brave1 marketplace after 150 prototypes were combat-tested.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Brave1's marketplace model compresses procurement from prototype to order, a model Western defense buyers are studying.
insights.locator: Ukraine has continued to fast follow

insights.claim: By late 2025 the drone contest was turning in Russia's favor as it outproduced Ukraine, but in early 2026 Ukrainian drone forces reportedly inflicted more casualties over four months than Russia could recruit.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Battlefield advantage oscillates rapidly, so no drone design or producer holds durable leadership.

insights.claim: Ukraine's Magura V5 became the first naval drone to sink an enemy warship in February 2024, and its USV campaign drove the Russian Black Sea Fleet from Sevastopol; Russia is expected to field more than 150 naval drones in 2026.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Uncrewed surface vessels are a proven, fast-growing naval segment drawing global emulation.

themes.theme: Interceptor drones and the cost curve

insights.claim: By February 2026 Ukrainian interceptor drones costing $800 to $3,000 each, such as Wild Hornets' Sting, accounted for about 70 percent of Shahed takedowns around Kyiv.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Cheap interceptors are displacing expensive SAMs for drone defense, threatening the missile-centric air-defense business model.
insights.locator: Interceptor Drones: A New Fast-Following

insights.claim: The U.S. Army acquired around 13,000 Merops interceptor drones at about $15,000 each, first used by Ukraine in 2024 and adopted by Poland and Romania, after collapsing a 16-step decision process.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Signals a large and rapidly procured U.S. market for low-cost interceptor drones.
insights.locator: The U.S. Army moved and evolved

insights.claim: Then-Army Secretary Dan Driscoll said Merops let the Army take down Shaheds costing $30,000 to $50,000, putting the U.S. on the right end of the cost curve.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Cost-exchange ratios now drive U.S. air-defense procurement priorities.
insights.quote: “take Shaheds down that cost $30,000 to $50,000, which is amazing because that puts us on the right end of the cost curve.”

insights.claim: After six U.S. personnel were killed in a drone strike in Kuwait in March 2026, 228 Ukrainian specialists deployed to Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE with interceptor drones, tactics and radar networks, an example of 'fast following as a service.'
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Ukraine is emerging as an exporter of combat-proven defense know-how and products, a potential growth story for its defense industry.
insights.locator: The Gulf States and the United States

insights.claim: The Ukrainian interceptor model has become one of the most widely emulated military innovations since early 2026, adopted in the Gulf, by the U.S. Army and in Japan, and Russia has copied it with the Yolka and interceptors mounted on An-2 and Yak-52 aircraft.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Global diffusion of interceptor drones points to a broad new procurement category across many militaries.

themes.theme: U.S. and Middle East: Shahed emulation and lag

insights.claim: The U.S. LUCAS one-way attack drone, built by Arizona-based SpektreWorks from a Shahed-136 training replica at about $35,000 per unit, was used by CENTCOM from the first day of Operation Epic Fury against Iran.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Cheap attrition munitions are entering U.S. inventories, opening a market for non-traditional defense manufacturers.
insights.locator: The United States and the Shahed

insights.claim: The U.S. took about three and a half years from the Shahed's demonstration point in Ukraine to combat use of LUCAS, fast by U.S. acquisition standards but slow versus the weeks-long Ukraine cycle.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: U.S. acquisition lag remains a structural constraint; firms able to compress it may win share.

insights.claim: The U.S. military's adoption of LUCAS shows it was willing to discard its preference for exquisite, high-cost munitions in favor of an adversary's cheap, good-enough weapon.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A cultural shift toward affordable mass could reallocate budget share from traditional primes' high-end munitions.
insights.locator: This is a clear example of fast

insights.claim: The Pentagon formed Task Force Scorpion Strike, its first dedicated one-way attack drone unit, followed in August 2026 by the multinational Task Force Falcon Strike in the Middle East.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Institutionalized attack-drone units imply recurring procurement rather than one-off buys.

insights.claim: Hezbollah fielded fiber-optic FPV drones against Israel about 18 months after Kursk, launching over 80 in several weeks with around 15 hits, while Israel had not fielded an effective counter despite the warning.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Even elite militaries lag on counters, suggesting underappreciated demand for counter-fiber-optic-drone solutions.
insights.quote: It demonstrates that even highly adaptive militaries can be slow followers when a lesson appears to belong to someone else’s war.

insights.claim: Russia transferred upgraded Shahed-type drones with Geran improvements and targeting intelligence to Iran for use against U.S. forces, per an August 2026 Institute for the Study of War report.
insights.speaker: CSIS
entities: Institute for the Study of War
insights.so_what: Bloc cooperation raises threat levels to U.S. Gulf bases and shipping, sustaining regional air-defense demand.

themes.theme: Western Pacific militaries learning from others' wars

insights.claim: The PLA conducted anticipatory fast following on August 6, 2026, using at least 13 armed KVD002 drones to strike fast-moving drone boats in training, rehearsing countermeasures to USVs that Taiwan is building.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: China is preparing to counter Taiwan's Ukraine-style USV strategy, raising the bar for Taiwanese maritime drone effectiveness.
insights.locator: Perhaps a more interesting example

insights.claim: PLA 81st Group Army units tested fiber-optic drones in 2025 within months of Kursk, and the PLA is developing networked robotic formations such as aerial swarms, ground wolf packs and maritime shark packs.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Chinese unmanned capability growth is a driver of allied Indo-Pacific drone and counter-drone spending.
insights.locator: ChinaThe People’s Liberation Army

insights.claim: Taiwan's executive proposed a $6.6 billion budget in June 2026 for domestically produced uncrewed systems, including 208,200 one-way attack drones, 1,446 reconnaissance drones and 1,320 USVs, after opposition parties had cut similar provisions.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A large domestic drone procurement program would benefit Taiwanese drone makers, contingent on legislative passage.

insights.claim: Japan's uncrewed defense funding rose from ¥111 billion in 2025 to ¥277 billion in 2026, targeting production of about 80,000 drones annually by 2030, with Terra Drone testing interceptor prototypes in Ukraine and deployments from 2027.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Japan's 2.5x drone budget increase is a sizable growth market for Japanese and partner drone makers.

insights.claim: An estimated 11,000 to 15,000 North Korean troops fought in and around Ukraine, gaining drone-war experience, and reports in 2026 indicate Russia is assisting North Korean military drone development.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Raises Korean Peninsula threat levels and supports South Korean and Japanese counter-drone investment.

insights.claim: Australia's April 2026 Integrated Investment Program allocated about A$12 billion over a decade to drones and uncrewed systems and up to A$7 billion for counter-drone capabilities, with early contracts including SYPAQ's Corvo Strike interceptor, though the author calls Australia a follower but not yet a fast one.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Australian drone and counter-drone budgets create opportunities for domestic suppliers like SYPAQ.

insights.claim: Taiwan's experience shows fast following is political as well as military: a military may identify the right lesson but cannot fast follow if national institutions cannot fund and authorize it quickly.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Legislative risk is a key variable for Taiwanese defense procurement timelines.

themes.theme: Implications and recommendations for Western militaries

insights.claim: The demonstration-to-adoption gap is driven by institutions rather than technology: weeks for Ukraine and Russia, about 18 months for Hezbollah, and about three and a half years for the U.S. Shahed copy.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Acquisition reform, not R&D, is the key lever for Western military adaptation and for vendor revenue timing.
insights.quote: The technology was equally available to all. What differed was institutional speed.
insights.locator: Second, the demonstration-to-adoption gap

insights.claim: Know-how travels mainly with people, as hardware can be copied from photographs but tacit knowledge of employment must be learned from those who have it.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Combat-proven operators and firms (notably Ukrainian) hold valuable, hard-to-replicate advantage in export markets.
insights.quote: Hardware can be copied from photographs. Tacit knowledge of how to employ it has to be learned or borrowed from those who already possess it.
insights.locator: Third, know-how travels mainly with people

insights.claim: The report recommends Western militaries create a standing intermediary linking users, industry and procurement with real authority and a protected budget, noting the Defense Innovation Unit and Australia's ASCA are only partial models.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Points to expanded rapid-procurement channels that favor agile, non-traditional defense suppliers.
insights.locator: Establish a dedicated intermediary

insights.claim: Militaries should establish standing rapid acquisition pathways that accept higher technical risk for speed, making this the norm rather than a wartime exception.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Rapid-acquisition normalization would shorten sales cycles for drone and counter-drone vendors.
insights.locator: Create emergency acquisition pathways

insights.claim: Military institutions should track and report to leaders and legislatures the time between a foreign innovation's demonstration point and fielding an equivalent or counter in their own force.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A visible adoption-gap metric could become a political driver for faster defense spending.
insights.quote: What is not measured is rarely improved.
insights.locator: Measure the demonstration-to-adoption gap

insights.claim: Fast following must be balanced with exploration, since an organization that only copies will always be one cycle behind the innovator it exploits.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Original R&D still matters; a pure fast-follower defense posture has limits.
insights.locator: Preserve exploration alongside fast following

insights.claim: The U.S. Army's decision to close its experimental drone battalion in favor of distributing drones across the force should be paired with an enduring doctrinal-laboratory institution.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Distribution of drones across the force implies broader, larger-volume Army drone procurement.
insights.locator: Institutionalize fast following in a doctrinal-laboratory
